title: Reading: Retro Communities Worth Following
content:
A second roundup, this one about where the writing actually is. Retro computing has good documentation and mediocre news coverage, and knowing the difference saves a lot of time.
Serious technical work. Pagetable.com does C64 and 128 hardware reverse engineering with disassembly and scanned original manuals, and it is close to the equivalent of reading a kernel source. Leaded Solder covers repair, restoration and bare-metal programming across Japanese and British machines. The MiSTer wiki is the best-written FPGA recreation documentation available, and its why FPGA page is a genuinely good explanation of the emulation versus replication distinction. The Retro Hacker is an FPGA MSX2 clone and a RISC-V console, which is the kind of thing that should be on an engineer’s desk.
Forums with actual engineers in them. VOGONS for retro PC hardware and DOS, which is the most technically serious of the Anglo-American forums. Retro Computing Forum for minicomputers and micros. Atari.org is still the definitive Atari resource. MSX is the central hub for MSX and has one of the better-maintained wikis in the hobby. Spectrum Computing is powered by a database, which means its information is structured rather than threaded.
Long-running personal blogs, which are consistently better than the magazines. Byte Cellar has been writing about vintage computing for years and covers conferences properly. Vintage Computing and Gaming is a blogazine with the same longevity. Bits By 8 does hardware deep dives. The Retro Hacker is an FPGA MSX2 clone and a RISC-V console, which is the kind of thing that should be on an engineer’s desk.
Databases, if you want to know what exists. Bitsavers for documentation, close to two terabytes of manuals, schematics and software. ZXDB via Spectrum Computing, which is the best-organised retro game database in existence. Gury’s Atari 8-bit Forever is a similar effort for Atari.
Events, if you are near one. VCF runs regional gatherings and is where the machines get switched on rather than discussed. Vintage Computer Festival covers the same ground in blog form.
A note on tone The retro computing community is unusually good at documenting what it does, and unusually bad at hedging. People reverse engineer a chip for a year and write it up in full. That habit is worth something professionally, and it is in noticeable contrast to how much of the infrastructure industry publishes.
If you are looking for the anti-pattern to avoid, it is not in these communities. It is in vendor blogs about a category the vendor invented.
